groups.name: Dynastinae
groups.description: Rhinoceros beetles form a subfamily of Scarabaeidae. The accounts below document oviposition, larval substrates, seasonal inactivity, and emergence for individual species.

groups.name: Lucanidae
groups.description: Stag beetles (Lucanidae). The account below documents oviposition and larval development in association with decayed hardwood.

groups.name: Rutelinae
groups.description: Shining leaf chafers form a subfamily of Scarabaeidae. These accounts distinguish adult foliage use from the substrates in which larvae develop.

groups.name: Cetoniinae
groups.description: Flower chafers form a subfamily of Scarabaeidae. The species accounts cover adult feeding, oviposition substrate, and pupal-cell formation.

groups.name: Cerambycidae
groups.description: Cerambycidae are longhorn beetles. The two accounts below concern members of Prioninae whose larvae develop in wood or wood-based substrates.

groups.name: Tenebrionidae
groups.description: Darkling beetles (Tenebrionidae). The records below describe captive development from egg to adult.

groups.name: Passalidae
groups.description: Bess beetles (Passalidae) occupy galleries in decaying wood. In the horned passalus, adults and larvae share a gallery and adults provision their offspring.

species.name: Pelidnota punctata
species.intro: A grape leaf feeds the adult, but a newly hatched grub needs decayed wood. A Kansas rearing study followed this spotted scarab from egg to adult over roughly two years.

sections.title: Adult food and egg laying
sections.text: Offer pesticide-free grape leaves to the adults. Pair the beetles where they can climb onto the foliage and watch at dusk, when they often mate. Set damp soil against decomposed hardwood for the female. Eggs have been recorded individually in moist soil beneath decaying wood.

sections.title: Raising the grubs
sections.text: Use soft, decomposed hardwood as the larval food. In Kansas, William Hayes placed hatchlings with crumbled, rotten elm in a large container and left the wood intact as the grubs developed. Elm is a documented choice. Grubs also occur in the decaying stumps and roots of other hardwoods.

sections.title: Timing the next generation
sections.text: Date the enclosure when eggs are laid and expect a long larval stage. Hayes followed one egg laid in early July to an adult in July two years later. In a larger sample of 21 pupae, the pupal stage lasted 13–24 days. These observations give two different time scales to track in a rearing log.

sources.title: W. P. Hayes (1925), Kansas Agricultural Experiment Station, Technical Bulletin 16
Angela Miner, Animal Diversity Web, Grapevine beetle
University of Minnesota Extension, Scarab beetles

species.name: Odontotaenius disjunctus
species.intro: Also called a bess beetle, this species raises its young in family galleries. The parents prepare food for the larvae and repair damaged pupal chambers.

sections.title: Set up a family log
sections.text: Give the family moist, rotted oak with enough intact wood for galleries. The University of Florida uses the same decayed oak in which the beetles were found for its classroom colonies. Maintain the moisture and add softened wood as the beetles consume it.

sections.title: Leave eggs with their parents
sections.text: Both adults tend the brood. They relocate eggs within the tunnels, and hatchlings share softened wood mixed with the colony’s frass. Preserve occupied galleries and their contents when adding food. Moving individual eggs or cleaning out all the frass takes away part of the rearing environment.

sections.title: Recognize pupal cells and new adults
sections.text: The family packs debris around each pupa. Leave those cells in place, including when an adult appears inside. Newly emerged adults are reddish and gradually turn black. Older siblings may help with brood care while they still share the log.

sources.title: C. S. Bibbs and colleagues, UF/IFAS Featured Creatures, Horned passalus
UF/IFAS Extension, Guide to Collecting and Maintaining Live Arthropods for Classroom Display

species.name: Tenebrio molitor
species.intro: A mealworm is the larva of a darkling beetle. With separate containers for breeding adults, growing larvae, and pupae, each stage is easy to follow.

sections.title: Prepare the trays
sections.text: Use a ventilated container with rolled oats or wheat bran. The grain serves as bedding and food. Add a small piece of carrot or potato as a moisture source and replace it before it spoils. Keep the containers covered so the grain stays clean.

sections.title: Start a dated batch
sections.text: Place adults on fresh bedding for an egg-laying period, then transfer the adults to a second tray. Label the first tray with the dates. The eggs and first larvae are tiny, so keep the used bedding even when it looks empty. One published rearing system used two-week laying periods.

sections.title: Collect pupae and emerging adults
sections.text: As larvae mature, pale, curled pupae appear among the grain. Move pupae to a ventilated container and transfer emerged beetles to an adult tray. The first pale adults will darken over several days. Keeping track of the trays lets you identify which adults produced each batch.

sources.title: Flinn Scientific, Culturing Mealworms, live material care guide
Yellow mealworms as an alternative animal feed source, Journal of Cleaner Production (2023), section 2.1
EAZA, Management Guideline Manual for Invertebrate Live Food Species, mealworm account

species.name: Gymnetis thula
species.intro: Adults visit flowers and feed on ripe fruit. The grubs grow in decaying plant material, where they eventually make a firm, oval chamber.

sections.title: House and feed the adults
sections.text: Use a covered enclosure with space above the substrate for the active beetles. They fly readily during the day. Offer ripe fruit for adult feeding. Wild individuals also visit sap flows and flowers.

sections.title: Provide a laying substrate
sections.text: Place decayed plant matter such as compost or fermenting oak wood below the feeding area. Females lay in this material and the hatchlings eat it. Keep a dated sample of the original substrate when checking for offspring so small larvae can continue to feed.

sections.title: Protect the pupal chambers
sections.text: Larvae pass through three instars before making oval earthen pupal cells. Set aside substrate containing complete cells and leave them intact through emergence. The LSU species account gives records of adults living up to eight months. Its detailed larval stage durations refer to other Gymnetis species, so use your own dates to track a G. thula brood.

sources.title: Louisiana State University AgCenter, Gymnetis thula, Harlequin Flower Beetle

species.name: Dynastes tityus
species.intro: Oak cavities supply this rhinoceros beetle’s grubs with a deep accumulation of decayed wood. The University of Kentucky has reared the species in a soil-and-wood mixture.

sections.title: Prepare a laying enclosure
sections.text: House a mated female in a secure, ventilated enclosure with room to burrow. The University of Kentucky guide uses at least a gallon of substrate and mixes two parts soil with one part rotten wood. Choose soil without pesticides or fertilizer. Provide pieces of bark or wood the adults can grip.

sections.title: Support larval feeding
sections.text: The grubs feed on the wood component as they grow. Keep enough soft, decayed hardwood in the enclosure to supply the larvae. In the wild they feed on the crumbly wood debris that gathers in oak cavities. Field development can span two or three years.

sections.title: Watch for a wandering grub
sections.text: When a mature grub begins wandering, the Kentucky rearing guide moves it into its own container with substrate for a pupal cell. A newly formed adult can remain below the surface for some time while its cuticle hardens. Record pupation and first surface activity as separate events.

sources.title: Bill Wallin, University of Kentucky Entomology, Rearing Eastern Hercules Beetles
University of Arkansas Arthropod Museum, Eastern Hercules beetle

species.name: Lucanus elaphus
species.intro: In Mississippi floodplain forests, researchers found giant stag beetle larvae both inside rotten logs and underneath them, where the wood touches soil.

sections.title: Build a wood–substrate interface
sections.text: Place pieces of moist, rotten hardwood in contact with the substrate. Benjamin Harink’s breeding account describes females laying eggs in the material beside the wood. Give the female access to both surfaces and keep track of the date she enters the laying enclosure.

sections.title: Feed developing larvae
sections.text: Harink reports raising the grubs on white-rotted wood or fermented beetle substrate. The Mississippi field study found larvae in logs with more than one kind of decay. Keep the food in contact with moist substrate and record which material each brood actually uses.

sections.title: Track identity through emergence
sections.text: Label each brood with its parentage. Closely related stag beetles can have very similar grubs. Researchers used DNA to confirm the identities of larvae from the wild. If you start from a known captive pairing, retain the link between each grub and its adults as it develops.

sources.title: Ulyshen and colleagues (2017), Ecology, genetics and distribution of Lucanus elaphus
Benjamin Harink, Ben’s Beetle Breeding Pages, Lucanus elaphus

species.name: Chrysina woodi
species.intro: One West Texas female laid 122 eggs in a single clutch. All 122 hatched in captivity.

sections.title: Oviposition
sections.text: The breeder housed the adults in a ventilated enclosure with approximately one gallon of lightly fermented flake soil. One female deposited her entire clutch in this substrate.

sections.title: Adult diet
sections.text: Adults fed on hickory foliage. The account also lists walnut and pecan as possible food plants. His account documents feeding on hickory.

sections.title: Larval development
sections.text: The original account recommends rearing larvae individually and providing red clay for pupation. He reports development to adulthood in approximately six months. Two wild-caught females survived for about one week and more than one month, respectively, after collection.

sources.title: Breeding Chrysina woodi, the jewel of Texas! (October 19, 2023)

species.name: Xyloryctes thestalus
species.intro: In the documented culture, adults ceased feeding from late October until April. Most eggs and larvae appeared between April and July.

sections.title: Breeding substrate
sections.text: The breeder used a ventilated enclosure with 4–5 inches (10–13 cm) of lightly fermented flake soil and bark on the surface. He kept the substrate slightly drier than that used for his other rhinoceros beetles.

sections.title: Adult feeding and seasonal inactivity
sections.text: Adults fed on apple and other firm fruits. They burrowed in late October and resumed feeding in April. The enclosure remained at approximately 68–75 °F (20–24 °C) during this period. Some wild-caught adults survived more than a year after collection.

sections.title: Offspring
sections.text: One egg laid before winter produced a male. The account records the remaining eggs or larvae between April and July and confirmed that captive-bred offspring reached adulthood.

sources.title: Breeding Xyloryctes thestalus at last!!!! (August 25, 2023, updated October 19, 2023)

species.name: Strategus aloeus
species.intro: Ox beetles were reared from larvae to adults in less than a year. One captive-bred male measured 53 mm.

sections.title: Adult feeding and oviposition
sections.text: The account reports substantial adult food consumption and recommended checking food at least every three days. Females laid eggs in several organic substrates.

sections.title: Larval substrate and pupation
sections.text: Larvae developed in organic raised-bed soil. The account recommends compacted topsoil for construction of pupal cells, although adults also emerged from containers without an added topsoil layer.

sections.title: Adult longevity
sections.text: The account records adult males surviving up to two years. The longest-lived female in his culture survived approximately nine months.

sources.title: Strategus aloeus – the Ox Beetle (December 3, 2022)

species.name: Mallodon dasystomus
species.intro: Eggs were deposited in damp sawdust. Larvae developed on hardwood sawdust prepared from pellets.

sections.title: Oviposition
sections.text: Adults laid eggs in approximately half an inch (1.3 cm) of damp sawdust. The account describes the eggs as hard-shelled and seed-like. This measurement refers to the laying layer.

sections.title: Larval food
sections.text: Larvae fed on hardwood sawdust prepared from expanded pellets. The original account also reported development in kinshi, sawdust colonized by fungal mycelium.

sections.title: Development
sections.text: The account gives a larval period of one to three years, depending on rearing conditions. The account reports that that larvae accepted supplementary protein and grew rapidly. The account does not specify the supplement or feeding schedule.

sources.title: Keeping Mallodon dasystomus – The Hardwood Stump Borer (December 1, 2022)

species.name: Stenodontes chevrolati
species.intro: In captivity, larvae reached maturity in about eight months on kinshi. Those reared on raw hardwood sawdust took about a year and a half to two years.

facts.title: Larval period
facts.text: 1–3 years in the breeder’s general account, with faster growth on kinshi

sections.title: Larval food and housing
sections.text: The breeder lists raw hardwood sawdust, kinshi (fungus-colonized substrate), and lightly fermented flake soil as larval foods. They recommend containers of at least 32 US fluid ounces (about 0.95 L) and prefer one-gallon jars (about 3.8 L).

sections.title: Adult feeding
sections.text: Adult feeding was not observed in this culture.

sources.title: Stenodontes chevrolati breeding account and follow-up, January 21–22, 2026 (Discord)

species.name: Dynastes grantii
species.intro: Larvae develop in decayed wood. In captivity, eggs can remain unhatched for several weeks after the female has finished laying.

sections.title: Egg laying and incubation
sections.text: Kim (2015) describes a breeding enclosure with 15–25 cm of moist substrate. After mating, he recommends moving the female to a second enclosure and leaving the eggs in place. His account gives an incubation interval of about two weeks to three months.

sections.title: Larval development
sections.text: BugGuide records larvae in rotten wood, including sycamore. Kim (2015) reports three larval instars and about 12–15 months from egg to adult under captive conditions.

sections.title: Adult feeding and longevity
sections.text: Krell and Krell (2015) kept one wild-caught male from Cochise County, Arizona, at room temperature with bark and wood chips and offered fresh apple approximately every four days. It survived nine months and one week after collection. Its age at capture was unknown.

sources.title: J. Kim (2015). A rearing guide to Dynastes grantii Horn, 1870. JKim’s Collections.
F.-T. Krell and V. H. I. Krell (2015). Longevity of the western Hercules beetle, Dynastes grantii Horn. The Coleopterists Bulletin 69, 760.
BugGuide, Dynastes grantii. Food and life history.
